newsitem.title: MONTSERRAT: Explosions brewing at Montserrat volcano.
newsitem.headline: Explosions brewing at Montserrat volcano.

text.p: New explosions at the killer Soufriere Hills volcano were brewing on Monday, officials on the beleaguered Caribbean island of Montserrat said.

Although the volcano was quiet, swarms of underground earthquakes were pushing up new lava, indicating more explosions were on the way, Montserrat Volcano Observatory deputy chief scientist Jill Norton said.

A thick plume of steam hung over the volcano's summit and ash filled the air in west Monsterrat, the island's Emergency Operations Centre said in a statement on activity from Sunday afternoon to Monday morning.
People were banned from entering the evacuated zone in the south and were warned to stay away from the volcano's flanks.
"We're somewhat relieved that the explosions have stopped, but everybody's watching and waiting. There is tension," Norton said.
"We've had a lot of earthquakes. They come and go in swarms -- one a minute for a period of two to five hours."
She said the earthquakes around the volcano were small, measuring less than three on the Richter scale, and caused no damage, but they indicated fresh lava was pushing to the surface.
The volcano exploded last week, sending rivers of debris into Montserrat's abandoned capital, Plymouth, setting houses ablaze and covering streets with thick volcanic ash.

Fires touched off by the "pyroclastic flows" of rock, ash and hot gases razed government headquarters, the customs office, public market and other landmark buildings. The fires were allowed to burn themselves out because the town was too dangerous for firefighters, officials said.
In June, lava flows from explosions killed nine people, devastated several villages and left 19 people missing and presumed dead.

Montserrat, a teardrop-shaped, 11-by-seven-mile (18-by-11-km) island in the eastern Caribbean, lived in harmony with its dormant volcano for nearly four centuries until it roared to life in July 1995.
